Extraction: Advancing Autonomous Incident Response: Leveraging LLMs and Cyber Threat Intelligence (title page, p. 1).

Amine Tellache (OODRIVE - Trusted Cloud Solutions, Paris, and L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle), Abdelaziz Amara Korba (L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle, and German University of Technology in Oman - GUtech), Amdjed Mokhtari and Horea Moldovan (both OODRIVE), and Yacine Ghamri-Doudane (L3i Lab, University of La Rochelle) (p. 1) — an industry-academic collaboration, with the system evaluated on the vendor's own enterprise SIEM alerts (§III.A, p. 4).
2025, GLOBECOM 2025 — IEEE Global Communications Conference, Communication & Information Systems Security track, proceedings pp. 25-30, DOI 10.1109/GLOBECOM59602.2025.11432623 (p. 1, footer).

Security teams performing incident response are overwhelmed by alert fatigue and high false-positive rates: SOC analysts face an average of 4,484 alerts per day and spend nearly three hours daily on manual triage (§I, p. 1, citing [2]). Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) could enrich and contextualize these alerts, but CTI is vast, heterogeneous, unstructured and fragmented across diverse sources, so searching, reading and correlating reports demands additional manual effort, highly skilled personnel and costly tooling, and is too slow for real-time attacks (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1). Multi-cloud environments add fragmented security models, and generic IR playbooks lack actionable guidance for less experienced teams (§I, p. 1). Existing LLM uses in CTI remain largely passive (summarization, TTP mapping), with a limited role in active incident response, while fine-tuning LLMs for continuously evolving CTI is costly (§I, p. 2).

A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based incident response framework that automates the workflows of SOC analysts, CTI analysts and incident responders (§II.A, p. 2; Fig. 1, p. 3). It takes a SIEM alert as input and runs two phases: (1) a hybrid Retrieval phase combining a standard search — an IOC Parser extracts domains, hashes, IPs and URLs, then queries private CTI platform APIs (VirusTotal in the experiments) for reputation, geolocation and historical malicious activity (§II.C, p. 3) — with an NLP similarity search over a Chroma vector database of embedded APT/cybercrime campaign reports from VX Underground, using an LLM-generated 'augmented alert' as the query and cosine similarity for matching (§II.B-II.C, p. 3; Eq. 1, p. 4; §III.A, p. 4); (2) an Augmented Generation phase in which a pre-trained LLM (GPT-4o) receives a structured prompt with the alert plus concatenated retrieved contexts and generates an incident response plan (§II.D, p. 4; Fig. 1b, p. 3). Agency is limited: the system is a single-LLM, single-pass RAG pipeline with tool-style API retrieval that produces a textual mitigation strategy for human responders — there is no autonomous execution of actions, no multi-step planning loop, no self-correction and no multi-agent orchestration (the only multi-LLM element is the evaluation ensemble, §III.B, pp. 4-5). The 'autonomous security operations' of the title is framed as a direction this work lays a foundation for (Abstract, p. 1), making it an advisory copilot for IR teams rather than an agentic responder. New CTI is integrated by re-embedding reports, avoiding fine-tuning (§II.A, pp. 2-3).

Design-and-evaluate study on two alert datasets (§III.A, p. 4): 100 real-world alerts randomly selected from the authors' company LogPoint SIEM between August 10 and September 8, 2024, and 10 simulated alerts generated in a controlled Proxmox test environment with an ELK-stack SIEM, Elastic Defend agents on Windows and Linux victim VMs, and MITRE Caldera emulating APT adversaries with ATT&CK TTPs (e.g., Automated Collection T1119, Exfiltration Over C2 Channel T1041, Process Discovery T1057, Process Injection T1055.002) (Fig. 2, p. 4). Evaluation uses a dual paradigm (§III.B, pp. 4-5): automated LLM-as-judge scoring on a 1-5 scale for three RAG metrics — Answer Relevance, Context Relevance and Groundedness — by three open models (Mistral-large-2407, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), each prompted to score and justify, cross-validated by a manual assessment from one in-house cybersecurity expert on the 10 simulated alerts (Table III, p. 6). There is no baseline condition (no comparison against unassisted analysts or another tool) and no time-to-respond measurement; all outcomes are response-quality scores (§III.C, pp. 5-6).

Not specified quantitatively — the paper measures no detection or response times and executes no empirical comparison against a concrete baseline (human analysts or an alternative system), so no comparative MTTD/MTTR benefit can be asserted (Art. I). The Abstract's claims of 'alleviating analyst workload and reducing response latency' (p. 1) are motivational, not measured. What is actually measured are LLM-judged quality scores on a 1-5 scale (§III.C, pp. 5-6): on 100 real-world alerts, Answer Relevance averages near 5 (e.g., 4.97 Mistral-large, 4.95 Llama-3.1-70B), Groundedness exceeds 4 (4.53, 4.19, 4.51), but Context Relevance is low at ~3.15-3.62 (Table I, p. 5), attributed to false-positive alerts and IOCs absent from VirusTotal; on 10 simulated (all true-positive) alerts, Context Relevance improves to ~4.0-4.55 (Table II, p. 5); the single-expert manual evaluation gives 4.20 Answer Relevance, 4.10 Context Relevance and 4.10 Groundedness (Table III, p. 6). These quality scores are the only empirical evidence; any MTTD/MTTR effect remains hypothetical.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Contribution to the agentic agenda is deliberate but modest: the paper argues for moving LLMs in CTI from passive tasks (summarization, TTP mapping) to active incident response (§I, p. 2) and demonstrates a reusable pattern — hybrid retrieval that fuses structured tool calls to CTI platform APIs with semantic search over an embedded CTI corpus, feeding a generation prompt (§II.C-II.D, pp. 3-4) — plus a fine-tuning-free adaptation strategy (continuous re-embedding of new CTI; §II.A, pp. 2-3). Its dual evaluation paradigm, using an ensemble of three LLM judges cross-validated by human experts, with the stated intent of later using automated scores as a filter to retain only accurate responses (§III.C.2, p. 5), is a transferable quality-gate design for agentic pipelines. However, the system itself exhibits limited agency — one retrieval-generation pass, no action execution, no inter-agent coordination — so it informs the perception/enrichment and advisory layers of future agentic IR systems rather than demonstrating autonomy; the authors position it as 'establishing a foundation for intelligent, adaptive cybersecurity frameworks' (Abstract, p. 1).

Acknowledged limitations: low Context Relevance on real-world alerts caused by false positives, IOCs not recognized in VirusTotal and CTI reports lacking detail on specific campaigns (§III.C.1, p. 5; §III.C.3, p. 6) — in those cases the system generates coherent output not grounded in retrieved context (§III.C.3, p. 6). Reviewer-noted gaps: no baseline comparison and no time/latency measurement despite the response-latency claim in the Abstract; only 10 simulated alerts and a single in-house expert validator (Table III, p. 6); LLM-as-judge scores from only three models with varying sensitivity (Table I, p. 5); GPT-4o selection justified by a leaderboard rather than task-specific comparison (§III.A, p. 4); vendor-internal alert data limits reproducibility. Future work (§III.C.1, p. 5; §IV, p. 6): add trusted private databases such as CrowdStrike and broader CTI report coverage; integrate the knowledge base with the OpenCTI platform (§II.B, p. 3); extend outputs to a wider range of cybersecurity roles and enhance model reasoning; and harden the system against adversarial attacks.

Partially on-construct: the paper targets the thesis domain (incident response in SOC operations) and the copilot intent — an LLM assistant that enriches alerts with CTI and drafts actionable response plans to relieve analyst workload (Abstract, p. 1; §II.A, p. 2) — and its hybrid RAG retrieval and LLM-judge-plus-expert evaluation design are directly reusable in the thesis's enrichment and quality-gate layers. However, it provides no MTTD/MTTR evidence (no baseline, no time metrics; §III, pp. 4-6) and exhibits limited agency: a single-pass advisory RAG pipeline without autonomous action, planning loops or multi-agent coordination (§II, pp. 2-4), so it supports the thesis's motivation and architecture chapters rather than its effectiveness claims. It enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat — the IEEE GLOBECOM conference series is an A4-stratum venue, so inclusion carries the qualification formalized in PDR-0006/0007 — and with the limited-agency caveat recorded in the cycle evaluation.

Medium — strong domain and copilot-intent match (CTI-grounded LLM assistant generating IR plans from SIEM alerts) with a reusable hybrid-RAG and dual-evaluation design, but it measures only LLM-judged response quality (Tables I-III, pp. 5-6), offers no MTTD/MTTR or baseline evidence, and the solution's agency is limited to single-pass advisory generation; the A4-stratum caveat (PDR-0006/0007) applies.
